questions.question: For affine quantization, what does the scale represent?
options: The real-value distance between adjacent quantized codes
The number of model layers
A guaranteed runtime speedup
The count of calibration examples
questions.explanation: Scale maps one integer-code step back into real-value space. A wider represented range usually produces a coarser step.

questions.question: Why must real zero be representable exactly in many integer schemes?
options: Operations such as zero padding rely on zero preserving its meaning
It makes every weight positive
It removes the need for calibration
It guarantees symmetric ranges
questions.explanation: If zero maps incorrectly, padding and other zero-valued semantics can introduce systematic error.

questions.question: What trade-off does a tighter calibration range make?
options: Finer in-range steps in exchange for more clipping risk
More metadata in exchange for fewer operators
Higher bit width in exchange for lower memory
Longer training in exchange for no evaluation
questions.explanation: Tightening the represented range reduces the scale, but values outside that range clamp to an endpoint.

questions.question: When is quantization-aware training a reasonable next step?
options: A supported PTQ path misses its quality budget and retraining is available
The target runtime has no compatible kernel
The deployment benchmark has not been defined
Only a smaller filename is required
questions.explanation: QAT can help parameters adapt to simulated rounding and clipping, but it cannot create missing runtime support.

questions.question: Why is successful export insufficient evidence of deployment support?
options: The runtime may execute unsupported operators at higher precision or insert conversions
Export always changes the task definition
Every exported model uses the same hardware
Calibration data is embedded in every graph
questions.explanation: Inspect the actual target execution plan because graph fallbacks and casts can erase the intended benefit.

questions.question: A candidate passes aggregate quality but fails a safety-critical slice. What should the release gate do?
options: Hold the release until the slice meets its explicit budget
Average the slice into the aggregate again
Ignore the slice because the file is smaller
Increase canary traffic to hide the difference
questions.explanation: Named high-cost slices are independent gates; an acceptable aggregate cannot waive their budgets.

questions.question: What makes a higher-precision artifact a usable rollback?
options: It is loadable under the same serving contract and its switch path is rehearsed
It has a similar filename
It was trained before the quantized model
It uses more disk space
questions.explanation: Rollback requires compatibility, availability, ownership, triggers, and an exercised traffic switch, not merely another file.
